this: this is what I am doing when I pay attention, and when you do it, you are doing the same thing.

what this means is that, you can think of the evidential boundary as the edge of your attention (as I have before), and as the edge of your conceptual capacity. as you work within the boundary, you are working to carve away at the edge of your attention, and you are working to sharpen the focus of that attention. as you push out, you push out the boundary of the world, and you push out the boundaries of your thought and your feeling. this is what is meant when people say that your mind is an organ that grows as it is used. this is the difference between, say, someone who was born blind, and a sighted person who is going blind in their old age. one person will grow blind as the organ of sight is not used (and, incidentally, the organ of vision will grow smaller), while the other person will grow blind as the organ of vision is used less and less and therefore the world of vision shrinks.

what happens, then, when you reach the edge of your world? this is, in practice, what people call an awakening. this is, in practice, what is meant when people talk about the ego dying.

## Suggested Reading

#### “The Tyranny of the Expected” — Ben Goldacre

“The idea is that if you look at your own behaviour, or you look at the things that you enjoy, or the things that you want to do, you could probably think of dozens of them in your head right now, and the vast majority of them are probably things that you never actually did. The things that you did are all the things that you had to do, whether that’s your job or your commitments, or whether that’s what other people expected you to do or what other people told you you should do. And so it’s very common, and a very important thing to realise, is that a lot of the things that you don’t do, you don’t do because of the tyranny of the expected.”

#### “Creativity Is Subtractive” — Grant Snider

“Sometimes the best way to be creative is to be selective and to take something away. As creators, we have a tendency to pile on more ideas. More words, more elements, more complexity. But creative work is more powerful if it’s more focused. Sometimes it’s better to pare something back.”
